limitations: The universe is the S&P 500 at each month end: large, liquid companies, where published anomalies are known to be weakest; the same engine can take a broader list.

The membership file (hanshof/sp500_constituents) ends at its last recorded change; months after it carry that list forward, are left out of the tests, and are marked where the book's readings use them.

Returns come from free price sources, downloaded by each company's current ticker, which often lack companies that were delisted or went bankrupt; the share of members with a return is reported, and a missing delisting return biases results toward survivors.

Stocks share industries and factors, so the bets are fewer than the stocks: the p-value comes from the month-to-month spread of the IC, which carries that dependence. The controls are size, momentum and value; industry is not among them, so a signal that only picks an industry can still pass.

Fundamentals come from XBRL company facts, which begin in 2009 for most companies; each value is the one first filed, but a filing date is a day, not a minute, so a value is used only if it was filed before the last trading day of the month. Revenue can be reported under different concepts in different years.

Two share classes of one company (GOOG and GOOGL) are one company in the tests. Share counts are put on one basis with split events from the price source; where the source gives none (Stooq), market value and share issuance can be off around a split. Classes worth different amounts per share (Berkshire's A and B) are added one for one, which misstates that company's size.
Ticker-to-company mapping uses the symbols insiders reported at the time and the SEC's current list; a reused ticker can be mismatched for a while, and unmatched members are counted and left out.
The 10b5-1 plan flag exists in the insider data sets only from 2023, so earlier planned sales and purchases count as discretionary.

Most of these signals were published before the sample begins, so the tests ask whether they still work, not whether they ever did (McLean and Pontiff 2016 find anomaly returns fall by about half after publication).
findings: 781 tickers that were in the S&P 500, tested from 2009-01 to 2025-08 (200 months, about 477 companies a month, 85% with a return), 800,664 insider transactions and the filings of 790 companies.

18 hypotheses tested (signals by horizon; 2 not testable), p-values from each signal's monthly IC series (the equal-weighted cosine test, which holds its size in short and autocorrelated series), Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05: 0 passed, 0 also held in the published direction, in both halves and after controlling for size, momentum and value. Of 50 random persistent signals, 8% had p below 0.05 (about 5% is the honest rate). Random tilts toward factors are not independent draws (effective number 2.9 of 50) and on real data can carry real factor premia, so their 2% below 0.05 is a reading, not a calibration; a reassignment permutation put 24% of them below 0.05.
Net share issuance, year over year (Pontiff and Woodgate 2008): mean rank IC -0.016 (t -2.0; controlled -0.011), p 0.0330, as published; the published long-short after costs: Sharpe 0.19.
Opportunistic insider buyers, last month (Cohen, Malloy and Pomorski 2012): mean rank IC 0.008 (t 1.6; controlled 0.011), p 0.1401, as published; the published long-short after costs: Sharpe 0.19.
Revenue growth acceleration (Jegadeesh and Livnat 2006): mean rank IC 0.008 (t 1.3; controlled 0.005), p 0.2381, as published; the published long-short after costs: Sharpe 0.03.

Earnings surprise against the same quarter a year earlier (SUE) (Bernard and Thomas 1989): mean rank IC 0.009 (t 1.3; controlled 0.010), p 0.2404, as published; the published long-short after costs: Sharpe -0.09.
Gross profit over assets (Novy-Marx 2013): mean rank IC 0.016 (t 1.4; controlled 0.006), p 0.2423, as published; the published long-short after costs: Sharpe 0.15.

Insider purchases as events: 8,402 purchases; over 20 trading days from the first tradable close the stock beat the universe by 0.06% against 0.15% on the same stocks' placebo dates (p 0.164, by month).
